newsitem.title: JAPAN: N.Korea's Kim says would deal with 'changed' South.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea's Kim says would deal with 'changed' South.

text.p: North Korea, hinting at a softening of its staunch refusal to negotiate with rival South Korea, said on Wednesday it would talk to Seoul if authorities took positive action to improve ties.

The statement, an official media excerpt of a treatise published on August 4 by leader Kim Jong-il, came a day after a group of U.S. lawmakers quoted North Korean officials as saying Pyongyang would never deal with the current Seoul government.

"If the South Korean authorities show a positive change in practice, we will sit face to face with them any time, have an open-hearted negotiation with them over the destiny of the nation and make efforts for national reunification hand in hand with them," said the report.
"We will follow what attitude and stand the South Korean authorities take and how they act," said the report, carried by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) and monitored in Tokyo.
Kim published the essay on reunification to mark the 52nd anniversary of Korea's liberation from Japanese colonial rule, which falls on August 15, KCNA said.
The Stalinist state's de facto leader called on Seoul to abolish its National Security Law, under which South Koreans are banned from making unauthorised trips to North Korea.

"The United States, a party directly responsible for the Korean issue, must completely change its anachronistic Korea policy and stop hindering the independent and peaceful reunification of Korea," the essay said.

Kim, who analysts say is likely later this year to formally take over the country his father Kim Il-sung founded in 1948 and ruled until his death three years ago, called on Washington to sign a peace treaty with North Korea.
The essay did not, however, mention U.S.-led efforts to start formal talks on a permanent peace arrangement to replace the fraying armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.

Also missing from the tract was any reference to North Korea's dire food shortage, which experts say threatens millions of lives. The United States and South Korea are the leading contributors of food aid to North Korea.

Preparatory talks to clear the way for peace negotiations involving the United States, China, North Korea and South Korea were held in New York last week but ended without final agreement. They are to resume on September 15.

On Tuesday, members of a U.S. congressional delegation said after a visit to the isolated communist state that North Korean officials they met were "adamant" in their refusal to deal with Seoul until the latter elects a new president in December.
"They absolutely want nothing to do with the present leadership," Porter Goss, chairman of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, told a news conference.
He said Pyongyang's unwillingness to engage Seoul stems from its anger at South Korean President Kim Young-sam's refusal to mourn the death of Kim Il-sung three years ago.
Kim Young-sam, whose five-year term ends in February and who is constitutionally barred from seeking a second term, is vilified almost daily in the North Korean official media.
